questions.question: When should an algorithm use Map instead of a plain JavaScript object?
questions.title: Map versus object for algorithm lookups
questions.direct_answer: Use Map when keys may be values other than strings, insertion order and size are part of the operation, or the data is a changing lookup table. Use a plain object for records with known string property names.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Map accepts keys of any value type.
Object keys are strings or symbols.
Map has `size`, `has`, `get`, and `set`.
Set is simpler when only membership matters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A plain object is designed mainly as a record with named properties, while `Map` is designed as a key-value collection. Map accepts values of any type as keys, reports its size directly, and has explicit `has`, `get`, `set`, and `delete` operations.

For example, a frequency table for array values can use `counts.set(value, (counts.get(value) ?? 0) + 1)`. A Map keeps numeric key `1` different from string key `'1'`; a normal object converts both property keys to strings.

Map is usually clearer for a changing algorithm lookup, especially when keys are objects or numbers. An object is natural for a fixed user record such as `{ name, email }`. If only presence matters, a Set communicates that requirement better than storing `true` values in either structure. Performance should be measured for unusual workloads rather than assumed from the type name.

sections.title: Collection keys and record properties
sections.content:
Objects inherit from a prototype unless created with `Object.create(null)`, so membership checks should use `Object.hasOwn`. Map has no inherited application keys and its iteration directly yields entries in insertion order.

Object identity remains important in a Map. Two separately created `{ id: 1 }` objects are different keys. When logical identity is an ID, use the ID itself as the key rather than expecting Map to compare object fields.

sections.title: Map, object, and Set
sections.content:
| Structure | Best meaning | Key behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Map | Changing key-value lookup | Any value as a key |
| Object | Record with named fields | String or symbol properties |
| Set | Membership or uniqueness | Each value stored once |

questions.question: How do you solve Two Sum with a hash map in JavaScript?
questions.title: One-pass Two Sum with complement lookup
questions.direct_answer: Scan the array once, store each earlier value with its index, and check whether `target - current` is already stored. Checking before insertion prevents one element from being used twice.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The needed partner is `target - value`.
Store values already seen with their indices.
Check before inserting the current item.
Return indices as soon as the complement exists.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two Sum asks for two different indices whose values add to a target. A Map removes the inner search: at each index, calculate the required complement and ask whether an earlier index stored it.

For example, with `[2, 7, 11, 15]` and target `9`, index 0 stores `2`. At index 1 the complement is `2`, which is already in the Map, so the result is `[0, 1]`.

The scan is O(n) average time and O(n) space. Check for the complement before storing the current value so a target such as `6` does not use the single `3` twice. If duplicates exist, storing the most recent index is usually fine for finding one pair; returning every pair requires a different result policy.

sections.title: Complements replace the nested search
sections.content:
The brute-force method tries every later element for every index, which is O(n²). The Map remembers all earlier candidates, turning the question 'have I already seen my partner?' into an average O(1) lookup.

The invariant is simple: before processing index i, the Map contains values only from indices smaller than i. Therefore, finding a complement automatically gives two distinct positions and preserves a clear one-pass proof.

questions.question: How do you build a character-frequency map in JavaScript?
questions.title: Character frequencies with Map
questions.direct_answer: Loop through the string and update each character with `(count.get(ch) ?? 0) + 1`. The resulting Map supports problems such as anagrams, first unique character, and most frequent character.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Begin a missing count at zero.
Increment once per character encountered.
Map avoids inherited object-property keys.
Text rules decide case and normalization.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A character-frequency map records how many times each character appears. The loop reads one character, gets its previous count or zero, and stores the count plus one.

For example, `banana` produces `b: 1`, `a: 3`, and `n: 2`. That table can then answer whether two strings have matching counts or which character occurs most often without scanning the original string again for every character.

Building the table is O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct characters. A `for...of` loop iterates Unicode code points, which is usually better than indexing UTF-16 units. Case-insensitive or accent-insensitive problems need an explicit normalization rule before counting, because the Map should reflect the question's definition of equality.

sections.title: Frequency tables as reusable evidence
sections.content:
A frequency table converts repeated searches into one preprocessing pass. Once built, each count lookup is average O(1), so several later questions can reuse the same evidence.

A plain object can also count known safe string keys, but `Object.hasOwn` or a null-prototype object avoids inherited names. Map keeps the collection API explicit and preserves the original key values.

questions.question: How do you group anagrams using a hash map?
questions.title: Group anagrams by a canonical signature
questions.direct_answer: Create the same canonical key for words with the same letter counts, store an array for each key in a Map, and append each word to its matching group. A sorted-character key is the simplest general signature.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Anagrams need the same canonical key.
Sorted characters are a simple signature.
The Map value is an array of matching words.
Normalization rules must be consistent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Grouping anagrams needs a key that is identical for words containing the same letters. The simplest key is the word's characters sorted into a stable order. A Map stores `signature → group of original words`.

For example, `eat`, `tea`, and `ate` all produce the key `aet`, while `tan` and `nat` produce `ant`. The algorithm keeps the original words in the arrays, so the output can be `[['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat']]`.

If the average word length is m, sorting makes the total roughly O(n · m log m). For a fixed alphabet, a count-based signature can reduce character work to O(m), but its key format must avoid ambiguity. Case, spaces, accents, and output order should be defined before normalization.

sections.title: Canonical keys turn matching into lookup
sections.content:
A canonical key removes irrelevant order while keeping relevant frequency. Simply using a Set of letters is wrong because `abb` and `ab` would look equal even though their counts differ.

A count signature can join fixed-position counts with separators, such as `1#2#0#...`. This is efficient for lowercase English letters but less general than sorting when the possible character set is large or unknown.

questions.question: How do you find the longest consecutive sequence with a Set?
questions.title: Longest consecutive sequence in linear average time
questions.direct_answer: Put every number in a Set, begin a scan only when `value - 1` is absent, and count upward while the next number exists. Starting only at sequence boundaries avoids repeating work.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Store every number in a Set.
A sequence starts when `value - 1` is absent.
Extend with `value + 1`, `value + 2`, and so on.
Duplicates disappear naturally in the Set.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Set solution treats each number as possible membership evidence. A number begins a sequence only when its predecessor is missing. From that true starting point, the algorithm counts consecutive values until the next value is absent.

For example, `[100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]` becomes a Set. Values `2`, `3`, and `4` are not starts because their predecessors exist. Value `1` starts the run `1, 2, 3, 4`, so the longest length is `4`.

Each number belongs to at most one forward run, giving O(n) average time and O(n) space with normal hash behavior. Sorting is an O(n log n) alternative that can use less auxiliary structure if mutation is allowed. Empty input returns zero, and duplicates should not increase a run's length.

sections.title: Sequence starts prevent repeated scanning
sections.content:
If the algorithm extends from every value, the same long run is counted many times. The missing-predecessor test supplies an invariant: only the smallest member can start that run.

Hash operations are described as average O(1), not an absolute mathematical guarantee for every implementation and input. Interview complexity normally uses the expected Set behavior; sorting remains a clear deterministic comparison.
